analytic.title: Modeling of Real-Time System Designs for Parametric Analysis

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In designing realtime software, system designers need to find out the time budget to allocate to each action of realtime tasks so that the tasks can meet their deadlines. Our solution to this problem involves representing the execution time of the actions as parameters, then analyzing the collaborative behavior of those realtime tasks. This paper proposes parametric timed models of realtime tasks whose executions are controlled by a scheduler. We develop an algorithm to synthesize a coherent model which represents the possible behavior from a set of realtime tasks by exhaustively searching their reachable states. A set of linear inequalities are then derived on the fly from the synthesized model as the condition of parameters for schedulability. By solving the inequalities using a constraint solver, we can obtain desirable values of the parameters. In addition, we have implemented the algorithm in a tool and conducted some experiments to show the effectiveness of our approach.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The application of model checking technique has been extended to realtime systems for reasoning and verifying timing properties in recent years [1,13,24]. Model checking tools for realtime systems, for example, UPPAAL, Kronos, and Verus [5,6,10], have been developed. However, most model checking techniques for realtime systems express quantitative information about time with concrete values.

In designing realtime systems, the information that system designers often want to know is the amount of time to be allocated to each system activity. It is sometimes necessary to calculate the time required for of a particular activity for some optimization purposes. More importantly, during the development process, tim-ing information of a system may change frequently as the design moves towards completion. It is inconvenient, inefficient, and inadequate to adopt model checking techniques that can only deal with concrete time or constant values to tackle these problems. For this reason, it is better to represent unknown or undecided time values with parameters, variables representing some fixed values, and do parametric analysis to obtain the possible values.

Fundamental principles of parametric analysis for realtime systems have been studied in [28,15,3,14], however, most of them focus on theoretical aspects. There are some practical difficulties in applying these principles to the design problems of practical realtime systems where we need to consider scheduling with details of scheduling primitives. Let us consider, for example, practical realtime software developed by a modern realtime programming language like Java with extended realtime specification (RTSJ).The system consists of a number of realtime tasks, and the executions of these tasks are managed by a realtime scheduler. Each realtime task is characterized by scheduling primitives such as priority, period, and deadline, for instance.

In our previous work [27], we proposed a parametric model checking method and parametric models called parametric timed structures which allow the use of variables on transitions to model execution times. The computing models of the previous work have insufficient support for scheduling issues which are needed to analyze the behavior of concurrently executing tasks, each of which is characterized by priority, period, deadline, and so on. We address this problem by introducing models that support scheduling concepts with built-in primitives for modeling realtime tasks straightforwardly as provided by the constructs in realtime programming languages.

In the realtime task models presented in this paper, we do not only focus on the schedulability issue, but also model the logical structure of each realtime task, i.e. the actions performed during task executions. In contrast to the timed automata approach which is typically used to analyze systems with complex timing, our modeling technique is straightforward in the way programmers develop realtime programs. This enables smooth translation from design models to implementation. We believe that this is an advantage of our models which can promote the application of a formal framework in the practical design of realtime systems. Additionally, even though we allow the use of parameters to represent execution time, in the algorithm, we need neither instantiating parameter values nor reasoning of arithmetic expressions using a decision procedure. This helps reducing the cost of the exhaustive search of reachable states.

The contribution of this paper is summarized as follows. First, we propose the models of periodic realtime tasks, called realtime task models (RTMs), to describe the design of realtime software with the use of parameters, and the composite realtime task model (CRTM) which renders the executions of the RTMs under all possible values of parameters. Second, we develop the synthesis algorithm that generates a CRTM from a set of RTMs. The algorithm considers all possible scheduling of the tasks for each disjoint conditions of parameter values. Third, we developed a tool which implements the synthesis algorithm and applied the tool in some examples to test the effectiveness of our modeling approach.

div.head: Related Works
div.p: Some recent works have considered automatic, dynamic analysis by exploring all possible behavior in a set of tasks as they are executing. Methods for scheduling analysis have been studied in [12,8,25,7]. These works use timed automata [2] to model tasks and use model checking tools such as Uppaal and HyTech to analyze the models. In [12], a program automaton is explicitly constructed for a multi-task program, and analyzed with HyTech. The case studies showed that the number of locations of the program automaton becomes large. In [8], Bradley et al. show how to construct a single timed automaton which models the interactions of a mixture of periodic tasks and tasks with message dependencies executed on multiple processors. In [25], Norström et al. consider scheduling of tasks with a fixed execution time and deadline which are triggered by events on a single processor. In [7], processes are modelled by constructing an automaton for each task, then delays are added to model the interference among tasks. These approaches provide safe estimations which are more accurate than rate monotonic analysis, and not as expensive as analysis on implementation.

Scheduling analysis using timed automata have been studied in [8,21,17,18]. An idea of task execution at locations in time automata are introduced in task automata [16]. Task automata are an extension of timed automata which associate each location of a timed automaton with a task for schedulability analysis. A task automaton is schedulable if there exists a scheduling strategy such that all associated tasks can be computed within their deadlines. TIMES is a tool for modeling and schedulability analysis based on task automata [4]. These works focus mainly on schedulability analysis using information of execution times, and parametric analysis is not supported.

The problem considered in this paper is very similar to the one considered in [17,11,19]. Fersman et al. [17] considers the schedulability checking problem for fixed priority scheduling and showed that this can be encoded into a reachability analysis problem on standard timed automata using two extra clocks to describe task arrival time.

In [11], Cimatti et al. adopted and generalized the method of [17] to use with parametric timed automata. They proposed a method for symbolically computing schedulability regions of realtime tasks scheduled using fixed priorities. The activation of jobs is modeled by a parametric timed automaton by associating activation events with transition labels, and a parametric time automaton is constructed for each task as schedulability checker. The region of parameter space that makes the system schedulable is computed by iterative algorithm enumerating all possible traces that could lead to an error state, then identifying, for each of the trace, the subsets of parameter space that are compatible with the trace. The conditions over the parameters of interest are computed and then joined together to produce the schedulability region of the system. The algorithm is not guaranteed to terminate in general cases, but converges for the case of periodic tasks. Frehse et al. [19] proposed an adaptation of counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) which is a method for using counterexamples to guide the construction of a set of good parameters for parameterized linear hybrid automata.

Each of these dynamic analysis methods shares the disadvantage that generating the model of scheduled tasks as timed automata is complex and, therefore, time consuming and prone to error. We reduce that cost by introducing less complex models, realtime task models (RTMs), to represent the behavior of each individual realtime task which is scheduled by preemptive priority-based scheduling policy. Program statements are abstracted to time-consuming transitions that is rep-resented by an action label and a duration of the transition. A parameterized RTM can have its durations represented using time parameters which can be concretized later to obtain a concrete RTM. For the analysis of the whole system, we generate a coherent model of scheduled tasks considering the timing of the tasks, priorities, periods, and deadlines. The generated model can then be analyzed automatically to derive the conditions of time parameters that allow the execution of scheduled tasks to meet their deadline. The models and methods we propose in this paper are restricted to periodic tasks, however, the extension to non periodic tasks is obvious by simulation [22]. Moreover, our approach considers both execution times and the scheduling characteristics of tasks in the task set.

div.head: Example
div.p: Consider a cruise speed control system of a train (shown in Figure 1) that has the following requirements. The system maintains the train speed at a speed preset by rail operator for safety. It consists of two parts: a speed sensor and an actuator. The speed sensor reads the current speed at a rate of 3 milliseconds. This period gives the deadline for reading the speed information. The actuator keeps the train at a speed preset by rail operator by accelerating or applying brakes to keep the train at the preset speed. The actuator operates at a rate of 7 milliseconds. Also, this period gives the deadline for executing the control loop. The speed control system is structured into two realtime tasks. The first task is the control task which performs the control loop based on the current speed obtained from the sensor. The second task is the sensor task which reads the information from the speed sensor.

The two tasks execute collaboratively performing different actions, i.e., read sensor, and accelerate or brake. The system designer wants to figure out the time budget for each action of both tasks that allows the tasks to satisfy their deadlines.

div.head: Approach Overview
div.p: The overview of our approach is shown in Figure 2. In our approach, the design of realtime software is considered as a set of realtime tasks running concurrently. To model realtime software, we use the models called realtime task models (RTMs). The modeling focuses on each individual task, for example, its scheduling characteristics and actions. Once we have the models of the realtime tasks, we compose them into a single coherent model called composite realtime task model (CRTM). The synthesis of CRTM is done by an algorithm which considers every possible condition of time parameters and the scheduling under such condition. The coherent model CRTM exhibits the behavior of all possible scheduled executions with respect to the conditions on time parameters. Then, we perform parametric analysis on CRTM, that is deriving the conditions of parameters for the schedulings that will satisfy the deadlines of the realtime tasks.

To build a model of a realtime task, we focus on the actions performed by the task, i.e., what does each action perform and how long does it take to complete? In our cruise speed control system, the control task and sensor task are modeled by the RTMs shown in Figure 3 and4, respectively. In the model, the control task has two actions, namely, accelerate and brake, whose duration are x 1 and x 2 . The sensor task has one action: read sensor, whose duration is x 3 . At this stage, the execution times of these three actions are undetermined, and left as time parameters: x 1 , x 2 , and x 3 .

The problem statement in this example is: what are the desirable values of x 1 , x 2 , and x 3 that allow the concurrent execution of the tasks to satisfy their deadlines? We solve this problem by synthesizing the CRTM of R A and R B and deriving the conditions for schedulability as linear inequalities of x 1 , x 2 , x 3 from the synthesized CRTM.

div.head: Preliminary Notations
div.p: Before we present the models for modeling realtime tasks in the following sections, we first define the basic notations used in our modeling approach for parametric analysis, namely, linear expressions, conditions, and assignment functions.
Linear expressions are used to represent the durations of transition in a realtime task model. We call the variables that are used in such linear expressions time parameters.

Definition 2 (Conditions) For a set X of time parameters, the set ψ(X) of parameter conditions c is defined inductively by:

To evaluate the value of the linear expression for quantitative reasoning, we need to assign concrete values to time parameters. An assignment function maps concrete values to time parameters. We also call the assigning of concrete values to time parameters concretizing.
Definition 3 (Assignment Functions) For a set X of time parameters, an assignment function γ : X → Z + is the function that maps each time parameter x i ∈ X to a positive integer value γ(x i ).

div.head: Our Models of Real-Time Software Design
div.p: In this paper, we assume that realtime tasks are periodic tasks running under fixed-priority scheduling algorithms. In general scheduling theory [9], a realtime task is characterized by the following parameters:

• priority: is the precedence of execution under scheduling; • period P: is the time interval between two consecutive releases; • release time Δ: is the time at which a task become ready for execution; • deadline d: is the time before which a task should be completed;

The release of a task is the request for execution when a task becomes ready. Each time a task becomes ready, it releases a periodic request. The successive release times (also called request times,arrival times, ready times) are at r k = Δ+kP, where r 0 = Δ is the first release and r k is the k + 1th release. The deadline d is relative deadline counted from each release, so it is required that the deadline must not exceed the period (d ≤ P). The successive absolute deadlines are at d k = r k + d, where d k is the absolute deadline of the k + 1th release. In general, periodic tasks usually have a deadline equal to period (d = P).

There is a special location wait in L at which a task waits for the next arrival of release time. Each label in Σ represents the action performed by the transition. There is a special action label wfnp in Σ for wait for next period. A task finishes a periodic execution when moved to the wait-location and waits there for the next release. When the release time arrives, the transition labeled by wfnp is taken to transit out from the wait-location and the execution of the next period begins.

A transition e = (l, σ , δ , l ) ∈ E represents the execution from a source location l ∈ L to a target location l ∈ L performing an action σ ∈ Σ whose duration is δ ∈ D(X). Durations representing execution time of the action are assumed to be more than zero, hence, we exclude Z - 0 . We define transition relation E with some restrictions to represent the structure of periodic tasks. First, we specify that a transition from wait-location is wfnp-transition only and wfnp-transition can only be used as a transition from the wait-location. Second, strongly connectivity and acyclic properties specify that an RTM must not contain any loops other than the loops formed by wfnp-transition.

Each individual RTM has its own scheduling information, however, after composition into a CRTM all scheduling information is represented in the CRTM as parameter conditions. The representation of scheduling information as parameter conditions by linear inequalities facilitates the analysis of parameter values in realtime system design problems. We can apply existing solvers to the inequalities for parametric analysis. This is an advantage of our approach.

The scheduling parameters sp = priority, Δ, P, d consists of: (1) priority of a realtime task is denoted by a number to indicate the precedence of execution. A higher number indicates higher precedence of execution. (2) Δ is the offset time at which the task is released for execution. (3) P is the interval of time between two consecutive releases. (4) d is the time before which the execution of the task is expected to complete. Note that a deadline of a periodic task is a relative deadline measuring from the release time of each period. Example. From the train cruise control problem we mentioned in Section 3.1, there are 3 actions: accelerate and brake are the actions performed by control task, and read sensor is the action performed by sensor task. We model the two tasks with RTM A and B as shown in Figures 3 and4. The scheduling parameters are given in the tables in both figures. The priority of B is defined to be higher than that of A. The deadlines of both tasks are assumed to be equal to their periods.

div.head: Composite Realtime Task Models
div.p: Realtime software consists of a set of realtime tasks executing concurrently. To analyze the behavior of the execution of realtime tasks, it is necessary to consider the scheduling of such tasks. A set of RTMs is to be composed into a composite realtime task model (CRTM) by considering the transition of the RTMs being scheduled based on different conditions on time parameters.
A CRTM is a labelled transition system defined as follows:

Definition 5 (Composite Realtime Task Model) Let R = {T 1 , . . . , T n } be a set of RTMs where Σ c is the union of the sets of action labels of all RTMs in R. We assume that no two different RTMs share the same action labels. E c is the labelled transition relation which represents the scheduled execution of the RTMs in R. There are 4 kinds of transition labels, namely, delay, release, execute and wait, which are described in the later section.
div.formula: T i = L i , l 0 i , Σ i , E i , sp i . A composite realtime task model C R = S, s 0 , Σ c , E c where • S is the set of states; • s 0 is the initial state; • Σ c = n i=1 Σ i is

div.head: States of CRTM.
div.p: From the viewpoint of a scheduler, an executing realtime task can be in one of three possible states: running, ready to run, or waiting. Initially, all tasks will be in their waiting state, and wait for the arrival of release time. Tasks can change states from ready to running under certain conditions, or from running to ready when preempted, or from running to waiting if the execution has finished.

The executions of RTMs are managed by a scheduler. Generally, a scheduler uses queues for maintaining scheduling information. In our approach, we define two queues, ready queue and waiting queue, used in the scheduling of RTMs executions.
Queues can be sorted by different properties. A ready queue is the queue sorted by the priorities of RTMs.

A waiting queue is the queue that is sorted by durations. A ready queue rq = [(T 1 , α 1 ), (T 2 , α 2 ), . . . , (T l r , α l r ).] T i ∈ R is the RTM that is ready for execution with relative deadline α i ∈ D(X). The RTM in the head element of the ready queue is the one with highest priority. Therefore, it is the RTM that is eligible for execution. A waiting queue wq = [(T 1 , β 1 ), (T 2 , β 2 ), . . . , (T l w , β l w )] where an element (T i , β i ) represents an instance of the RTM T i ∈ R waiting to be released with relative release time β i ∈ D(X). The RTM in the head element of waiting queue is the one with lowest relative release time and thus will be the next RTM to be released. We define states of CRTM as follow.
Definition 6 (States of CRTM) Let C R be a composite realtime task model, a state s in an execution sequence of C R is a tuple: s = (t, l, rq, wq) where
div.formula: • t ∈ D(X) is parametric time at current state; • l ∈ ∏ i∈I L i

div.head: is composite location at current state; • rq is the ready queue at current state;
div.p: • wq is the waiting queue at current state.

The states of the tasks are represented in the ready queue and the waiting queue. Initial state s 0 is the state with initial time t 0 = 0, initial composite location l0 = (wait 1 , . . . , wait n ) where each RTM is initially at its wait-location, rq is empty, and all RTMs are in wq waiting with their release times.

div.head: Definition 7 (Configuration) Given
div.p: a state s = (t, l, rq, wq) of a CRTM, the configuration of a state s is the tuple of components in s excluding current time t. The configuration of s is denoted by config(s) where: config(s) = ( l, rq, wq).

There can be two or more similar states with identical configurations at different time in a CRTM because of periodic execution. So, we regard two different states to be equivalent by their configurations.

div.head: Definition 8 (Equivalence of States) Any two states s and s of a CRTM are equivalent if and only if config(s) = config(s ).
div.p: Let s = (t, l, rq, wq) and s = (t , l , rq , wq ), the states s and s are equivalent if and only if 1. l and l are identical, 2. rq and rq are identical, and 3. wq and wq are identical.

div.head: Transitions of CRTM.
div.p: A CRTM may take different types of transitions depending on the current configurations of the ready queue and waiting queue. There are 4 types of transitions a CRTM may take, namely, delay, release, execute, and wait. At a given state, the possible types of transitions depend on the configurations of ready queue and waiting queue. We omit the formal definition of the transition of CRTM due to space limitation. The formal definition and transition rules is given in [26]. We use the following figures to show the corresponding changes of state for each type of transitions. A state of CRTM is represented by a box with parametric time, composite location, ready queue, and waiting queue shown inside, respectively.

div.head: Synthesizing of CRTM
div.p: RTMs are parametric models and we allow the durations in the models to be represented by parameters. The possible transitions from a state may depend on the values of parameters in the models. The synthesis algorithm considers all possible schedulings of the given set of RTMs.

An executing realtime task can be in one of three possible states: running, ready to run, or waiting. Initially, each task will be in its waiting state waiting for the arrival of its release time. It can change from ready to running under certain conditions, or from running to ready if preempted, or from running to waiting if the execution has completed.

div.head: CRTM Synthesis Algorithm
div.p: The RTM to be executed is determined according to the state of the scheduler, that is, the queue configurations and elapsed time. The scheduler is defined as follow.

div.head: Definition 9 (Scheduling Function) For a CRTM C R scheduling function Sched C R : S → 2 E c maps a state s ∈ S to a subset of transitions E c according to the transition rules.
div.p: As the time information in RTMs can be parameterized, a possible execution of RTMs depends on the conditions of parameters. Therefore, the RTM to be executed is represented by the conditions of time parameters used in the RTMs. All possible executions associated with conditions are encoded in the CRTM. The algorithm for synthesizing CRTM from a set of RTMs R = {T 1 , . . . , T n } is shown in Algorithm 1. The algorithm generates conditions of parameters on-the-fly while applying transitions for the feasible scheduling in stateless depth-first search manner starting from initial state s 0 without remembering state space (stateless). Initially, the ready queue rq is empty and the waiting queue wq is initialized to be released by the release time of each realtime task T i . The stack TO VISIT is used to keep track of the states from which transitions will be generated. The use of stack TO VISIT brings about the generation of transitions in depth-first-search manner. In each call of search routine, a state s is popped from stack TO VISIT and the transitions from s are generated. For each generated transition, target state s i is checked by config in stack (line 17), whether a state with the identical configuration is already contained in stack TO VISIT or not. If a configuration is identical to that of s is already in TO VISIT, we put s to TERMINAL, the set that marks the states where repetition of transition sequences happens, and skip to the next iteration. Otherwise, the target state s i is pushed to TO VISIT, and transitions from s i are further generated recursively.

div.head: Deriving Parameter Conditions
div.p: There are two kinds of conditions that can be derived from a CRTM. The first one is a deadline condition, i.e., the weakest condition required for a state to satisfy tasks' deadlines. The second one is a path condition, i.e., the condition required to make the current transition path valid. A deadline condition can be derived from a state, and a path condition can be derived from a transition. The deadline condition for state s is denoted by dc(s) where dc(s) = (α 1 > 0) ∧ (α 2 > 0) ∧ . . . ∧ (α l r > 0). Deadline condition of a state s requires that the relative deadlines of all running tasks in the ready queue be greater than zero. This is the weakest condition for all running tasks to satisfy their deadlines in state s.
A path condition υ is denoted by pc(υ) where

, for a delay-transition and execute-transition, • pc(υ) = (β 1 ≤ 0), for release-transition, • pc(υ) = true, for wait-transition Transitions of a CRTM are generated with condition of time parameters. For delay-transition and execute-transition, it is required that the release time of the next task to be released has not arrived, that is β 1 > 0. On the other hand, for release-transition, it is required that the release time of the next task to be released has arrived, that is β 1 ≤ 0.

We note that it is sufficient to specify a path condition using only the next relative release time (β 1 in wq), because a waiting queue is sorted so that the smallest relative release time is at the head of the queue, and only one task can be released at a time.

div.head: Termination, Soundness and Completeness
div.p: In this section, we discuss about the properties of the composite model CRTM generated by the synthesis algorithm, and termination of the algorithm (Theorem 1). Interesting properties of the synthesized CRTM are summarized in Theorem 2 and Theorem 3. The CRTM generated by the synthesis algorithm yields conditions of parameters that make the concurrent executions of the RTMs satisfy their deadlines (Theorem 2). If there exists a parameter assignment that allows the concurrent executions of the RTMs satisfy their deadlines, such assignment will be included in the parameter conditions yielded from CRTM synthesis algorithm (Theorem 3). The proofs of this theorems are given in [26]. We briefly describe about the termination and omit the proofs here due to space limitation.

During the search in the synthesis algorithm, a transition path can become infinite. We show an infinite transition sequence from the speed control example in Figure 6. A transition path can become infinite because no equivalent states are found along the path. In our observation, we found that the paths which do not have delay transitions will grow infinitely.

We observed that contradiction of parameter conditions happens in the paths which have no delay transition between two consecutive release transitions. To exclude such paths, we define the scheduling function Sched C R in the algorithm not to generate two consecutive release transitions without a delay transition.

Since scheduling function Sched C R generates transitions with delay between two consecutive releases of the same task, we found that such paths with infinitely many delay transitions will eventually reach a repeated configuration. That is, the if-statement at line 17 will eventually become false, and TO VISIT set will get smaller and eventually become empty. Hence, the CRTM synthesis algorithm terminates.

Theorem 3 (Completeness) Let π |γ be the concrete execution path of a concrete system C S , tsc be the total schedulability condition derived from the corresponding CRTM, then for any assignment γ, if deadline satisfaction ds(π |γ ) = true, then γ |= tsc holds. This theorem says that if a concrete system concretized by assignment γ meets their deadlines, the assignment function γ satisfies the total schedulability condition derived from the corresponding CRTM.

div.head: Tool
div.p: We have implemented the CRTM synthesis algorithm in a tool using Java to experiment and evaluate our proposed method. The tool reads description of a set of realtime task models as input from a file, generates the composite model according to the given parameters and scheduling information, and then computes the conditions of time parameters for the models to satisfy the deadlines. The tool can output the generated CRTM as an output file in DOT language [20] for visualizing. We use Graphviz [23], an open source tool to draw graphs from generated DOT files in PDF format. We can zoom in to see a specific parametric conditions. The visualization helps us in understanding the behavior of the CRTM and inspecting the choices of parametric conditions. The CRTM of the speed control example is visualized as shown in Figure 5. We applied our tool on some small examples. The results of our experiment is shown in Table 1 The derived schedulability conditions are to be used as input to a constraint solver or by assigning values to some or all of the time parameters in the conditions and evaluate the truth value or simplify the conditions.

div.p: These conditions provide the information about relations among the time parameters. If we choose the values of time parameters to satisfy one of these conditions, such values will make the concurrent execution of the two tasks to satisfy their deadlines. We can apply the existing mathematical tools to obtain the desired values of the parameters.

In our experiment, we use the derived conditions as input and use Mathematica to reduce the system of linear inequalities and solve the reduced inequalities. The solution of (x 1 , x 2 , x 3 ) that satisfy the deadlines obtained from the inequalities in these conditions are any values of assignment γ ∈ {(1, 1, 1), (1, 1, 2), (1, 2, 1), (2, 1, 1)}.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: A practical design model should be able to straightforwardly described the timing and scheduling characteristics of realtime tasks such as execution times, deadlines, periods and priorities. The models we proposed in this paper enjoy the built-in notions of scheduling and time parameters which facilitate the modeling of realtime tasks and the analysis of timing properties such as schedulability. In our framework, we model individual RTMs, then synthesize a coherent composite model CRTM which represents all schedulable possibilities of the concurrent executions according to the conditions of parameter values. The execution of RTMs managed by a scheduler changes dynamically as the executions progress. Such dynamic change makes the analysis difficult. However, the scheduling of RTMs is encoded as conditions of parameters in CRTM. As a result, the parametric analysis of timing properties can be performed using the conditions in CRTM.

In our parametric models, we represent undecided values of execution times in the design with parameters and later we are to figure out the suitable values of parameters to achieve the schedulability. The composition algorithm synthesizes a single coherent model which represent the collaborating execution of a set of realtime tasks. The composition can handle the use of parameters to represent duration of execution time in RTMs. The algorithm adds a parameter condition for each possibility of scheduling which depends on parameter values. There is a pattern for an infinite execution path and we found that the parameter conditions derived on an infinite execution paths is contradicted. Therefore, we statically exclude such infinite paths from the synthesis algorithm to prune away unnecessary searches and establish finiteness in CRTM.

Another advantage of our parametric approach is that we can use parameter conditions for some optimization purposes using techniques such as linear programming. The parameter conditions derived from the experiments using our tool suggests this feasibility.

div.head: Conclusions and Future Works
div.p: In this paper, we presented a method of using parametric analysis technique for modeling and analyzing the design of realtime systems. We proposed parametric timed models, namely, realtime task models (RTMs) for modeling periodic realtime tasks executing under the control of a scheduler, thus each of which has scheduling parameters such as priority, release time, period, and deadline.

To analyze the collaborative behavior, it is necessary to obtain all possible behaviors of such parametric timed models. We developed an algorithm to synthesize a composite realtime task model (CRTM), a coherent model which represent the possible behaviors, from a set of RTMs, by exhaustively searching their reachable states. CRTM will be used in the parametric analysis for obtaining the values of parameters which ensure that each RTM will meet its deadline, thus the entire system is schedulable. The parametric analysis is achieved by deriving linear inequalities encoded in CRTM and analyzing them using existing constraint solvers.

Even though the parametric timed models have parameters, in the algorithm, we need neither concretizing parameter values nor reasoning in arithmetic expressions using a decision procedure. This lowers the cost for the exhaustive search of reachable states.

We implemented the algorithm in a tool and use it to evaluate the method using two examples to show feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed method. The improvement of the tool to integrate some constraint solvers and experiment on larger case studies are in future work.

In our previous work [27], we have proposed a parametric model checking method. The model in this work is different from CRTM in that it does not have transition conditions. However, it is possible to extend the method so that such model can be used with conditions We plan for the extension of our model checking algorithms to deal with the models that transitions incorporate a condition in future work. Moreover, as we did not take the concept of release or execution jitter into consideration, an extension to handle this could make the modeling even more realistic.
